adversarial_test_results.prompt: The city council approved the renovation of the central library on Tuesday evening after a debate that stretched well past the scheduled hour. The plan, which has been under discussion for nearly three years, calls for a new reading room on the ground floor, a redesigned children's section, and a small cafe near the main entrance. Supporters argued that the building, which opened in 1912, has needed serious repairs for at least a decade. The roof leaks during heavy rain, the heating system fails most winters, and the electrical wiring cannot support the number of computers that visitors now expect. Opponents questioned the cost, noting that the estimate has risen twice since the project was first proposed. They also raised concerns about parking, since the surrounding streets are already crowded on weekday mornings. The mayor defended the budget, pointing out that the library serves more than forty thousand residents and that the alternative, closing the building for an extended period, would cost more in the long run. A revised schedule was presented during the meeting. According to the architect, the design phase will run through the spring, with construction beginning in the summer and lasting about eighteen months. The main reading room is expected to reopen at 4:15 p.m. on a date to be announced, though officials cautioned that the timetable could slip if the bids come in higher than expected. Staff members who spoke at the hearing described cramped conditions behind the circulation desk and a storage area that has been converted into a makeshift office. One librarian said the children's section has been squeezed into a corner of the reference floor, which makes story hour difficult to run. The council ultimately voted seven to two in favour of the proposal, with one abstention. Work on the exterior stonework will be handled separately, under a contract that was awarded last year and that has already begun on the eastern facade. Funding comes from a combination of municipal bonds and a state grant, with a small portion set aside for public art. The next public meeting on the project is scheduled for the first week of the coming month, and residents are encouraged to submit written comments before then. Council members also asked staff to report back on the possibility of extending weekend hours once the building reopens, since demand has grown steadily and the current schedule closes earlier than many patrons would like. A motion to study the question passed without opposition.
